newsitem.title: UK: Dlr makes little headway in Europe, but tone firm.
newsitem.headline: Dlr makes little headway in Europe, but tone firm.

text.p: The dollar was near the day's highs against the mark and yen in late European trade after spending the session trapped in narrow ranges, with operators keeping a watchful eye on the U.S. stock and bond markets.

Sentiment was still bullish, but traders said the market was loath to drive the dollar up for now for several reasons -- its almost straight-line rally last week, nervousness about U.S. asset markets, and a series of U.S. economic data due this week.
"The dollar's still bid overall, for instance, I don't see it going below 1.7180 (marks) today. We're just waiting because we need more information," said one trader at a U.S. bank.

The dollar was at 1.7230/37 marks at 1545 GMT, off its session high but up from 1.7178/88 in late European trade on Friday. Dollar/yen was at 126.44/48, also off its high but above Friday's 125.75/85.

Traders said the market was steering clear of pushing dollar/yen up in the face of Japanese authorities' continued warnings about "excessive" currency moves, though they believed solo intervention by Japan would not damage the dollar much.
"Everyone still wants to buy dollars, but at the same time they're a bit cautious about all this talk about possible intervention," said a trader at a Japanese bank.

"I think we'll head up later this week and see if they're serious about intervention. If they don't do anything we'll see the dollar go higher, and if they do, we'll have a great opportunity to buy dollars on dips," he said.

For much of the day, European currency traders had been hesitant to move the dollar as they waited for the U.S. stock market to open, nervous after the Dow plunged 148 points on Friday following strong inflation data.
Both dollar/yen and dollar/mark were buoyed in Europe's afternoon as the Dow began the day on a soft note, with traders relieved that Friday's selloff had not continued.

U.S. Treasuries were steady as well, following a drop on Friday on the inflation data. But a strong dollar could discourage foreign investors from buying U.S. bonds, said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at Monument Derivatives in London.
"If one assesses the U.S. bond market in foreign currency terms, the higher the dollar goes, the more overvalued they (U.S. bonds) become," Lewis said.
The market was now looking ahead to a medley of U.S. data due this week for hints on the prospects of a U.S. interest rate rise at the Federal Reserve's policy-making meeting in May.

"There's a modest degree of upside for the dollar, as we think some of the figures coming out this week will be dollar-supportive...although we're not looking for a major move in the dollar at this stage," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi International here.
"The question is not so much whether the market has priced in the hike we think is coming (at the Fed's May meeting) but whether it's priced in more," Richardson said.

Elsewhere, the British pound hit a new 4-1/2 year high of 2.8052 marks in early trade. But it backed off later in the day while sterling/dollar also weakened, as milder-than-expected UK producer price data dampened speculation of a sharp interest rate hike in the UK.
Sterling/mark was at 2.7965/74 in late European trade against 2.8000/10 late on Friday, while cable was at $1.6220/30 against $1.6290/00.
